2001 Diophantine Sextuples of small height
--------------------------------------------

The following table lists 2001 Diophantine sextuples of small height as discovered by various authors.

The sextuples are listed as bracketed [a,b,c,d,e,f] where a-f may be an integer or most likely a rational number.

The Diophantine m-tuple has the property that the product of any two fractions + 1 is a square. In a sextuple, there are 15 such possible product pairs, i.e., ab+1, ac+1, etc., ..., ef+1, all summing to a square.

The 2001 sextuples are sorted uniquely, then arranged in ascending numerical order and indexed.

Following the example in Phil E. Gibbs' table[1] listed in his Annex A, each sextuple has a classification scheme which is indicated by symbols indicating the algebraic relationships between the six fractions or terms.

The letters in round braces, e.g. "(a,c,d,f)", indicate Diophantine sub-tuples which are regular pairs, triples, quadruples and quintuples [2]. If the letters appear in square brackets e.g "[a,c,d,f]" this means that the reciprocals of the numbers satisfy the equation for a regular m-tuple.

Regular sextuples are also shown in square brackets since in this case the inverses always also satisfy the same equation [3].

The possibility that a product of fractions equals one was also tested and was indicated in the one case (990) where it occurred with [abcd = 1].

There are 20 possible Diophantine triples for a Diophantine sextuple where each triple can create a unique elliptic curve.

A special relationship for a triple embedded in the sextuple is indicated as "Z6x2<<a,b,c>>" for the case when the induced elliptic curve has torsion group Z6 × Z2 with the result that it can be extended to a rational Diophantine sextuple containing three regular quintuples. In this case, there are an infinite number of sextuples occurring for the curve.

The other special relationship for a triple is indicated as "Z4x2<<a,b,c>>" where the elliptic curve has torsion group Z4 x Z2. There are two very interesting cases (359), and (954) where the Diophantine sextuple has both a triple with Z6 x Z2 torsion and a triple with Z4 x Z2 torsion (but not the same triple).

All other non-denoted 39,740 triples from the 2001 sextuples induce elliptic curves of torsion group Z2 x Z2. There are 263 triples inducing a Z6 x Z2 torsion group and 17 triples inducing a Z4 x Z2 torsion group for a total of 40,020 triples embedded in the 2001 sextuples. 

Another relationship equivalent to (abcd − 1)2 = 4(ab + 1)(cd + 1) is indicated by "<<a,b|c,d>>" . When this condition is met the two extensions of the quadruple to a quintuple form a sextuple with two regular quintuples and two regular quadruples.

A check was also made to locate any strong Diophantine triples, listed as "ST(a,b,c)", if they exist, but none was found in this list of 2001 sextuples. In fact no Diophantine sextuple has been found yet, containing a strong Diophantine triple nor has even a Diophantine strong quadruple been found yet.

Finally the known author(s) of each sextuple is attributed by "{1-9}" parenthesis where the value indicates which author to properly attribute. There were some sextuples which were discovered by more than one author.

References
-----------
[1] Phil E. Gibbs, https://www.researchgate.net/publication/309429323_A_Survey_of_Rational_Diophantine_Sextuples_of_Low_Height
[2] Phil E. Gibbs, “Some rational Diophantine sextuples”, Glas. Mat. Ser. III 41 (2006), 195-203
[3] Philip E Gibbs, “Regular Rational Diophantine Sextuples”, viXra:1609.0425 (2016)
